exact_relevant_excerpts.excerpt:
## Statement

Assume AC. Let $\mu\sim N(\mu_0,\tau_0^2)$ with $\tau_0^2>0$, and, conditional
on $\mu$, let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$ be IID $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with known
$\sigma^2>0$ and $n\ge1$. The sampling data use $n$-dimensional Lebesgue
measure. For every $y_{1:n}\in\mathbb R^n$, define
$$V_n=(\tau_0^{-2}+n\sigma^{-2})^{-1},\qquad \mu_n=V_n\left(\frac{\mu_0}{\tau_0^2} +\frac{n\bar y}{\sigma^2}\right),\qquad \bar y=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^ny_i.$$
The evidence is finite and positive, and the posterior is $N(\mu_n,V_n)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, $\mu_0\in\mathbb R$, $\tau_0^2,\sigma^2>0$, $n\ge1$, and
observed real data $y_1,\ldots,y_n$.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is assumed by the Gaussian density normalization supplier. [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F1] The normal law $N(m,v)$ for $v>0$ has density $(2\pi v)^{-1/2}\exp(-(x-m)^2/(2v))$. [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]].

[F2] This normal density integrates to one under AC. [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]].

[F3] A proper prior probability and parameter-measurable sampling probability kernel constitute a Bayesian model. [[def-bayesian-model-as-prior-and-sampling-kernel]].

[F4] Evidence is the prior integral of the joint likelihood section; the normalized quotient is introduced only on finite positive evidence. [[def-posterior-evidence-normalizer-and-fiberwise-update]].

[F5] The likelihood-weighted prior can be normalized to a probability exactly when evidence is finite and positive. [[prop-fiberwise-posterior-propriety-iff-finite-positive-evidence]].

[F6] The dominated Bayes formula identifies the normalized density quotient as a posterior kernel. [[thm-bayes-formula-for-dominated-kernels]].

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement and observed data $y_{1:n}$.

1.1 Put $P=\tau_0^{-2}+n\sigma^{-2}>0$, $q=\mu_0\tau_0^{-2}+\sigma^{-2}\sum_i y_i$, and $r=\mu_0^2\tau_0^{-2}+\sigma^{-2}\sum_i y_i^2$. The product of the proper normal prior density and the $n$ normal likelihood densities [F1] is $C\exp\{-\tfrac12(P\mu^2-2q\mu+r)\},\qquad C=(2\pi\tau_0^2)^{-1/2}(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-n/2}>0.$ The densities are jointly measurable, so the specified model is a Bayesian model by [F3]. [A1, F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Completing the square gives $P\mu^2-2q\mu+r=P(\mu-q/P)^2+\Delta$, where $\Delta=r-q^2/P\ge0$ because the left side is a sum of nonnegative weighted squares and at $\mu=q/P$ equals $\Delta$. Hence the evidence is $C e^{-\Delta/2}\sqrt{2\pi/P}.$ It is finite and strictly positive; the Gaussian integral follows by scaling the normalized density in [F1]–[F2]. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Dividing the likelihood times prior in step 1.1 by the evidence computed in the preceding step gives the density $\sqrt{P/(2\pi)}\exp\{-P(\mu-q/P)^2/2\},$ which is $N(q/P,1/P)$. Since $1/P=V_n$ and $q/P=\mu_n$, this is the stated posterior. Finite-positive evidence is the valid domain by [F4] and [F5], and [F6] supplies the posterior-kernel identity; [F2] normalizes the resulting Gaussian density. [A1, F1, F2, F4, F5, F6, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the normal specialization of [[def-hierarchical-bayesian-model]] with
parameter space $\Theta=\mathbb R$ and hyperparameter space
$H=\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)$. Fix $\mu\in\mathbb R$ and $\tau^2>0$.
Conditional on $(\mu,\tau^2)$, let the
group parameters be independent with $\theta_j\sim N(\mu,\tau^2)$. Let the
observed group summaries be conditionally independent with
$\bar Y_j\mid\theta_j\sim N(\theta_j,s_j^2)$, where each known $s_j^2>0$.
Then, conditional on $(\mu,\tau^2,\bar Y_1=\bar y_1,\ldots,\bar Y_m=\bar y_m)$,
the $\theta_j$ are independent and
$$\theta_j\sim N(\hat\theta_j,V_j),\qquad\hat\theta_j=\frac{\bar y_j/s_j^2+\mu/\tau^2}{1/s_j^2+1/\tau^2},\qquad V_j=\left(1/s_j^2+1/\tau^2\right)^{-1}.$$
If $(\mu,\tau^2)$ is unknown with a proper hyperprior supported on
$\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)$, let $P_y$ be the full posterior kernel from
[[thm-hierarchical-posterior-normalization-on-positive-finite-evidence]] and,
on each positive finite evidence fiber, define its hyperparameter marginal on
Borel $C\subseteq H$ by $\Pi_y(C):=P_y(C\times\mathbb R^m)$. The posterior law of
$\theta_j$ is the mixture of these conditional normal laws over $\Pi_y$;
replacing $\mu,\tau^2$ by point estimates is not this posterior. No normalized
hyperparameter posterior is asserted on a zero or infinite evidence fiber.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** specialize the BCS-03 Normal–Normal update to each group, factor the finite conditional posterior, and integrate over the hyperparameter posterior.

**Given:** The stated fixed hyperparameters, group summaries, and variances.

1.1 Fix a group $j$ and specialize [F5] to one observation: identify its parameter with $\theta_j$, set $\mu_0=\mu$, $\tau_0^2=\tau^2$, $n=1$, $y_1=\bar y_j$, and $\sigma^2=s_j^2$. The model in [F1] supplies this normal prior and sampling law, while [A1] and [A2] verify the choice and positive-variance hypotheses of [F5]. The theorem gives a finite positive group evidence and posterior variance $V_j=(1/\tau^2+1/s_j^2)^{-1}$ and mean $\hat\theta_j=V_j(\mu/\tau^2+\bar y_j/s_j^2)$, as stated. [A1, A2, F1, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 For each group put $\mu_j(A)=\int_A f_j(\theta,\bar y_j)N(\mu,\tau^2)(d\theta)$ and let $m_j=\mu_j(\mathbb R)>0$. By [F5] and step 1.1, $\mu_j/m_j=Q_j=N(\hat\theta_j,V_j)$. Apply [F3] to the hierarchy with the proper point-mass hyperprior at the fixed $(\mu,\tau^2)$. Its latent prior on $\mathbb R^m$ is the product of the group priors by [F1], and its likelihood density is $\prod_j f_j(\theta_j,\bar y_j)$ by [F2]. Repeated Tonelli [F4] shows that the normalized posterior assigns each measurable rectangle $\prod_j A_j$ mass $\prod_j\mu_j(A_j)/\prod_jm_j=\prod_jQ_j(A_j)$. The posterior and $\bigotimes_j Q_j$ are probability measures agreeing on the generating rectangle pi-system; the constant exhaustion by the full space has common finite mass one, so [F6] makes them equal. This proves conditional independence and the displayed formula for every group. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Now suppose $(\mu,\tau^2)$ is random with a proper hyperprior supported on $H$. For each $(\mu,\tau^2)$, let $m_j(\mu,\tau^2)$ be the positive finite group evidence computed in step 1.1. Tonelli [F4] gives $Z(y)=\int_H\prod_jm_j(\mu,\tau^2)\,\Pi(d\mu,d\tau^2)$; when $0<Z(y)<\infty$, the marginal hyperparameter posterior is $\Pi_y(d\mu,d\tau^2)=Z(y)^{-1}\prod_jm_j(\mu,\tau^2)\Pi(d\mu,d\tau^2)$. By [F3], the full posterior has this hyperparameter marginal and the conditional groupwise laws from step 2.1. Integrating the indicator of a Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R$ first over the group parameters and then over $(\mu,\tau^2)$ gives $\Pr(\theta_j\in A\mid y)=\int_H N(\hat\theta_j(\mu,\tau^2),V_j(\tau^2))(A)\,\Pi_y(d\mu,d\tau^2)$. This averages over the full hyperparameter posterior rather than substituting a point estimate. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $\mathcal Y=\prod_{j=1}^m\mathcal Y_j$ be the data space and
$\mathcal Y_+=\{y\in\mathcal Y:0<Z(y)<\infty\}$ its measurable subset of
positive finite evidence fibers. Write $P_y$ for the full latent probability
kernel supplied by
[[thm-hierarchical-posterior-normalization-on-positive-finite-evidence]], and
set $\Lambda_y:=P_y$ for every $y\in\mathcal Y$. On $\mathcal Y_+$ this is
the normalized joint posterior; off $\mathcal Y_+$ it is the prior filler
$P_0$, so no likelihood quotient is formed there. For an already observed
group $j$, its **current-group posterior predictive law** for a future
observation with the same conditional observation kernel is
$$Q^{\mathrm{cur}}_{j,y}(A)=\int_\Xi K_j(\theta_j,A)\,\Lambda_y(d\eta,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m).$$

For a new group, specify a probability kernel $K_{\mathrm{new}}$ from
$(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to a future observation space
$(\widetilde{\mathcal Y},\widetilde{\mathcal A})$. Its **new-group posterior
predictive law** is
$$Q^{\mathrm{new}}_y(A)=\int_\Xi\left[\int_\Theta K_{\mathrm{new}}(\theta,A)\,G_\eta(d\theta)\right]\,\Lambda_y(d\eta,d\theta_1\cdots d\theta_m).$$
For $y\in\mathcal Y_+$, if $\Lambda_y^\eta$ denotes the hyperparameter
marginal of $\Lambda_y$, the joint posterior law of
$(\eta,\theta_{\mathrm{new}})$ used here is
$\Lambda_y^\eta(d\eta)G_\eta(d\theta_{\mathrm{new}})$. Thus the new-group
prediction first draws a new latent parameter from $G_\eta$ and then draws its
observation from $K_{\mathrm{new}}$. On $\mathcal Y_+$ both formulas average
over the joint posterior and retain uncertainty about unknown hyperparameters.
On exceptional fibers they reduce to prior-predictive laws because
$\Lambda_y=P_0$.

## Statement

Under [[def-hierarchical-bayesian-model]], the current-group and new-group
predictive assignments of
[[def-current-and-new-group-posterior-predictive-laws]] are probability
kernels on the full data space $\mathcal Y$. On every positive finite evidence
fiber they are the stated posterior-predictive laws. On zero or infinite
evidence fibers, the posterior kernel uses its prior filler, so the predictions
are the corresponding prior-predictive laws. When a future current-group
observation is drawn from $K_j$ conditional on the latent tuple, or a future
new-group parameter is first drawn from $G_\eta$ and then observed from
$K_{\mathrm{new}}$, these kernels are conditional laws of the future
observations given the observed data. This is a posterior-predictive statement
under the specified model, not a frequentist coverage claim.

## Example

Take one group with $\theta\mid t\sim N(0,t)$ and $Y\mid\theta\sim N(\theta,1)$, where $t=\tau^2>0$. Observe $y=0$, but replace the proper hyperprior in [[def-hierarchical-bayesian-model]] by the improper measure $\Pi(dt)=t^{-1}dt$ on $(0,\infty)$. Its evidence-weighted density is not integrable, so it cannot be normalized to a posterior probability. This is a warning example outside the proper-hyperprior hypotheses of the hierarchical posterior theorem.

## Example

Let the hyperparameter be $t=\tau^2\in\{1,4\}$ with prior probability
$1/2$ at each value. There is one group, $\theta\mid t\sim N(0,t)$, and
$Y\mid\theta\sim N(\theta,1)$. Observe $y=0$. The full posterior for $\theta$
is a mixture of the two conditional normal posteriors. Plugging in the
posterior mode of $t$ instead yields just one component, which is not the full
posterior.

## Example

In the known-variance normal hierarchy, fix $\mu$, an observed group summary
$\bar y_j$, and $s_j^2>0$. For finite $\tau^2>0$, the posterior mean is a
strictly weighted average of $\bar y_j$ and $\mu$. As $\tau^2\downarrow0$ it
approaches complete pooling at $\mu$; at the boundary $\tau^2=0$, the prior
itself forces $\theta_j=\mu$. As $\tau^2\to\infty$, the posterior mean and
variance approach the group-only values $\bar y_j$ and $s_j^2$, the
no-pooling limit. The value $\tau^2=\infty$ is not an admissible proper prior.
